vignette:
Mei presents with a quiet, meticulous composure that seems at odds with the turmoil she describes. At 74, her posture is perfect, her words chosen with the precision of the software engineer she was for over four decades. She speaks of her life as if it were a system she designed—logical, orderly, with predictable inputs and outputs. It was her husband of fifty years, Kenji, who finally convinced her to seek help, after finding her awake at 3 a.m. for the third time in a week, staring at the wall, her hands clenched so tightly her knuckles were white.

The disruption, the bug in her system, began forty years ago. Her son, David, was eight. Mei remembers the exact date the world tilted off its axis. It was a Tuesday. David had been lethargic, bruising easily. She’d assumed it was a virus, a normal childhood ailment. The diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia was a catastrophic system failure for which she had no protocol. Her world, built on logic and control, dissolved into a terrifying landscape of variables she couldn't manage: white blood cell counts, chemotherapy protocols, the odds of survival.

For two years, the pediatric oncology ward of the hospital became their home. Mei describes this time not in a linear narrative, but in a series of sensory fragments that still ambush her. The sharp, sterile smell of antiseptic that can suddenly flood her senses while she’s washing dishes. The rhythmic, insistent beeping of the IV pump that she sometimes hears in the silence of her own home, a phantom sound that makes her heart pound. Most vivid is the image of David’s small, pale face against the stark white of the hospital pillow, his hair gone, his eyes looking too large for his head. She spent countless nights in a vinyl recliner by his bed, watching the rise and fall of his chest, her mind a frantic loop of “what ifs” and bargains with a universe she no longer trusted.

David survived. He is now a healthy man with a wife and two children of his own. The outcome was positive, the problem solved. For decades, Mei believed she had successfully compartmentalized the trauma. She threw herself into her work, finding solace in the clean, binary certainty of code. In her professional life, every problem had a solution, a patch, a workaround. She could debug the most complex systems, imposing order on chaos. It was a refuge.

Retirement, two years ago, took that refuge away. Without the demanding structure of her career, the firewall she had built around the memories began to crumble. The quiet of her days gives the intrusive thoughts room to grow. Last month, her six-year-old grandson developed a fever and a cough. While her daughter-in-law saw a common cold, Mei was plunged back into the terror of the hospital. She couldn't sleep, convinced his cough was the prelude to something catastrophic. She found herself hovering, checking his temperature obsessively, unable to quell the panic rising in her chest.

She is perpetually braced for disaster. A phone call after 9 p.m. sends a jolt of pure adrenaline through her. She avoids medical dramas on television and feels a wave of nausea if she has to drive past the hospital. She feels profoundly disconnected from the joy her family should bring her. When she looks at her healthy, thriving son, she sometimes doesn't see the successful architect before her, but the frail, eight-year-old boy, and the guilt is immediate and overwhelming—guilt that she couldn't protect him, guilt that she is still so broken when he is so whole. Her mind, once her greatest asset for solving problems, now feels like a prison, running the same traumatic loop over and over, a piece of corrupted code she cannot find and cannot fix.
